payload.rationale: No current data were supplied, so this rests on background knowledge through early 2026 plus extrapolation. The US recorded roughly 1,800–2,000 confirmed measles cases in 2025 (highest since 1992), and 2026 began at a faster pace: the large South Carolina Upstate outbreak and the Utah/Arizona outbreak carried several hundred cases into January, and national counts by late winter 2026 appeared to be running well ahead of the equivalent 2025 period, with continuous transmission threatening US elimination status. A plausible central expectation for the 2026 CDC total is roughly 2,500–4,500 cases, with seasonal waning in summer typically slowing accrual. Exceeding 6,000 would require either sustained multi-state outbreaks through the fall or a new very large outbreak in an under-vaccinated community, which is possible but not the base case. Reasons the estimate could be too high: measles outbreaks in the US usually burn out after exhausting susceptibles in affected communities, summer/fall transmission is lower, and the 2025 total, despite alarm, stayed under 2,000. Reasons it could be too low: I lack the actual count through mid-September 2026; if early-2026 momentum (several hundred cases per month) persisted or expanded into additional low-coverage regions, 6,000 could already be within reach, and declining vaccination coverage plus imported cases from Canada/Mexico raise the tail. Also the CDC's count as of expiration (not later revisions) is what matters, which slightly favors lower reported totals.
limitations: No supplied evidence; no knowledge of actual CDC case counts after early 2026.
Extrapolation from partial-year trends is highly uncertain for outbreak-driven counts.
Exact CDC reporting timing and revision policy could affect the settled value.
